key_insight: Inverse PINNs can recover Manning friction reliably in 2D shallow-water flows with sparse noisy data, but 1D cases reveal a structural bias that data quantity alone cannot fix.
engineering_relevance: For hydrodynamic inverse modeling, the study defines when sparse depth-velocity measurements are sufficient for trustworthy friction calibration and when alternative identification methods are needed.
method: Benchmarked inverse PINNs on two shallow-water test cases: 1D MacDonald channel and 2D sloped channel.
Treated Manning friction as a trainable positive scalar, learned jointly with the flow field using a two-phase training strategy.
Varied observation sparsity, noise level, and observed variable type (depth, velocity, or both).
evidence_signal: In the 2D case, friction error stayed below 5% with at least 10 depth and velocity observations and noise up to 10% of the field standard deviation, while 1D estimates retained a roughly 15% positive bias across settings.
watch_item: Recovery degrades sharply when only depth or only velocity is observed, so joint observability and identifiability checks are essential before using inverse PINNs in practice.
paper_title: How Sparse and How Noisy? Systematic Benchmarking of Inverse Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Manning Friction Estimation in Shallow Water Equations
